text:
Diversity and Evolution of Life
CELL – STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION
CELL – STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION
All organisms are composed of structural and functional units of life called 'cells'. The body of some organisms like bacteria, protozoans and some algae is made up of a single cell whereas the body of higher fungi, plants and animals are composed of many cells. Human body is built of about one trillion cells.
Cells vary in size and structure as they are specialized to perform different functions. But the basic components of the cell are common to all biological cells. This lesson deals with the structure common to all types of the cells. You will also learn about the kinds of cell division and the processes involved therein in this lesson.
summary: Cells are the fundamental units of life, varying in size and specialization but sharing common basic components. All cells, whether from single-celled organisms like bacteria or complex multicellular organisms like humans, contain essential structures such as the cell membrane, cytoplasm, and DNA. This lesson explores these universal cellular components and introduces the two main types of cell division: mitosis and meiosis, which are crucial for growth, repair, and reproduction.

subject: Biology
subsection: Landmarks in the study of a cell
text: Soon after Anton Van Leeuwenhoek invented the microscope, Robert Hooke in 1665 observed a piece of cork under the microscope and found it to be made of small compartments which he called "cells" (Latin cell = small room). In 1672, Leeuwenhoek observed bacteria, sperms and red blood corpuscles, all of which were cells. Much later, in 1831, Robert Brown, an Englishman observed that all cells had a centrally positioned body which he termed the nucleus.
summary: Robert Hooke observed the structure of cork using a microscope and coined the term "cell" to describe its small compartments. Soon after, Anton van Leeuwenhoek used the microscope to discover various cellular structures including bacteria, sperm, and red blood cells. In 1831, Robert Brown observed the central body in cells and named it the nucleus.

Chloroplast versus mitochondria
Can you now visualize how these two organelles are opposite to each other, one traps the solar energy locking it in a complex molecule (by photosynthesis), the other releases the energy by breaking the complex molecule (by respiration).
Similarities between mitochondria and chloroplasts: both contain their own DNA (the genetic material) as well as their own RNA (for protein synthesis). Thus, they can self-duplicate to produce more of their own kind without the help of nucleus.
Thought the chloroplasts and mitochondria contain their own DNA the hereditary molecule and also their own ribosomes, they are termed as semi-autonomous only because they are incapable of independent existence outside the cytoplasm for a long time. Since most of their proteins are synthesised with the help of the nuclear DNA.
summary: Chloroplasts and mitochondria are opposite yet complementary organelles; chloroplasts capture solar energy through photosynthesis, storing it in molecules, while mitochondria release this energy through respiration by breaking down those molecules. Both organelles share similarities in containing their own DNA and RNA, allowing them to replicate independently, but they remain semi-autonomous as most of their proteins are encoded by nuclear DNA and synthesized within the cell.

text:
A single cell divides many times and forms a multicelled organism. Unicellular bacteria and protozoa divide and increase in number. The injured tissues are replaced by new cells through cell division. Thus cell division is one of the most important activities in all organisms. In this lesson you will study about the two kinds of cell division and the processes involved in them.
Majority of cells in a multicellular organism grow and then can divide. However, the cells like the nerve and muscle cells of animals and guard cells of plants do not divide.
The process of cell division is almost same in all organisms. A cell passes through phases of growth after which are able to duplicate their chromosomes before they divide. These phases in the life of a cell constitute the cell cycle.
summary: Cell division is a fundamental process in all organisms, enabling the formation of multicellular structures from single cells and replacing damaged tissues. This process involves a series of phases including growth and duplication of chromosomes, culminating in cell division. Not all cells in a multicellular organism have the ability to divide; for instance, nerve and muscle cells in animals and guard cells in plants remain post-mitotic.

subject: Biology
text:
You can use the term mother or parent cell for the cell that undergoes division and the daughter cells for the ones that are the result of this division. Before each daughter cell undergoes division, it must grow to the same size as its mother cell. We can distinguish two main phases in the life of a cell.
The interval between two successive cell divisions is termed interphase (phase at which the cell is not dividing). It is the longest period in the cell cycle (Fig.4.11). The interphase is subdivided into three main periods - G_1, S and G_2.
G_1 (Gap-1 ) Phase i.e. First phase of growth – This is the longest phase. Lot of protein and RNA are synthesised during this phase.
S or synthetic Phase - It comes next. Lot of DNA is (synthesised). A chromosome contains a single double helical strand of DNA molecule. After S-phase each chromosome becomes longitudinally double except at centromere,
and thus, it has two molecules of DNA and two chromatids. Thus each chromatid contains one molecule of DNA. The two chromatids are joined by a centromere (which does not divide at this stage) to form a single chromosome.
G<sub>2</sub> (GAP 2) phase - More protein including the histones are synthesised in this phase. Cytoplasmic organelles such as mitochondria and golgi bodies get duplicated. Centriole also divides into two centrioles contained in a single centrosome.
(ii) M-phase or dividing phase - Represented by the symbol M (Mitosis or meiosis) (Fig. 4.11). Mitosis occurs so that during this period the chromatids separate and form daughter chromosomes. The daughter chromosomes go to daughter nuclei and cytoplasm divides forming two identical daughter cells.
BIOLOGY
summary: The cell cycle consists of interphase and the M-phase. Interphase, the longest part of the cell cycle, includes the G1 phase for growth, the S phase for DNA synthesis, and the G2 phase for further growth and organelle duplication. During the M-phase, mitosis occurs, where sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles of the cell, followed by cytokinesis to form two genetically identical daughter cells.

summary: Mitotic cell division involves two main processes: karyokinesis and cytokinesis. During karyokinesis, the nucleus divides through prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase, resulting in the formation of two identical daughter nuclei. Cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm, leading to the formation of two daughter cells. This process ensures that each new cell receives an exact copy of the genetic material, maintaining cellular identity and function.

What is a karyotype
Chromosomes can be seen distinctly only at metaphase. They are then photographed, cut and arranged in pairs according to size. Such an arrangement of homologous chromosomes of an individual in descending order according to size, is termed as a karyotype (see human karyotype in lesson 21).
